Supplementary Material

In the supplementary material, we describe the theory, architecture, datasets, optimisation, and engineering that underpin Hamilton-Zero. SS1 covers variational principles on spinor manifolds, with a full exposition on the theory behind our automatic-differentiation primitives of Lie derivatives, the Peter-Weyl theorem that shows why our model has support on a larger manifold than NQS, as well as how our variational principle manages the case of non-linear quaternionic functions through a Casimir-operator-based regulariser and energy penalty that preserves the spin-1/21/2 variational principle. Next SS2 describes Hamilton-Zero’s architecture, drawing parallels and design choices from large-scale pretraining runs of large-language models. Here we also describe the router we use to learn entanglement structure through deep reinforcement learning, characterise its automorphism-orbit entropy, as well as the tree tensor-network-style contraction mechanism that is conditioned on the model’s embeddings of interaction data. Next, we describe in full detail the pretraining routines and datasets we used in SS3. We then describe in SS4 our state-of-the-art sampling scheme for MCMC on the configuration manifold S​U​(2)NSU(2)^{N}, our energy kernels, and our extension of the KFAC optimiser, all of which we made shard-mappable and GEMM-optimised for training on Nvidia H200 GPUs.

S1 Variational principles on Spinor Manifolds

S1.1 From basis amplitudes to wavefunctions on SU​(2)N\mathrm{SU}(2)^{N}

The standard spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} wavefunction is a complex-valued function on {+,−}N\{+,-\}^{N}, equivalently a vector Ψ∈ℂ2N\Psi\in\mathbb{C}^{2^{N}} with one amplitude per computational-basis configuration. Two features of this picture constrain every method built on it. The dimension is exponential in NN, and the domain is discrete. Thus a Hamiltonian acts through explicit sums over connected configurations, enumerated anew for each interaction structure. Tensor networks and NQS address the first constraint by replacing the 2N2^{N}-dimensional space with a lower-dimensional variational sub-manifold. The second constraint they inherit unchanged however, and it is what ties each trained model to one Hamiltonian’s connectivity. The central objective of this section is to remove both at once, by replacing the discrete domain with the continuous group manifold SU​(2)N\mathrm{SU}(2)^{N}, on which Hamiltonians act by differentiation.

Tensor networks and neural quantum states replace the exponentially large Hilbert space by a lower-dimensional variational family [115, 140], but the resulting optimisation can still be limited by stability and trainability. On the quantum-circuit side, barren plateaus provide a distinct failure mode in which gradient variance can vanish exponentially with system size [20].

The central objective of this section is to expose the methods that allow us to sidestep both the curse of dimensionality and the curse of linearity, by replacing the discrete domain of the spin-1/21/2 basis vectors with a continuous Lie group domain. The wavefunctions we employ,

ψ:(SU⁡(2))N→ℂ,\psi:\bigl(\mathrm{SU}(2)\bigr)^{N}\to\mathbb{C}, (S1.1)

are smooth functions on the Lie group manifold. Here, each spin is parametrised by a unit quaternion qi∈S3q_{i}\in S^{3} via the standard identification SU⁡(2)≅S3\mathrm{SU}(2)\cong S^{3} embedded in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}. Hence any neural network model in our framework thus consumes 4​N4N continuous inputs for NN bodies which is linear in NN.

As usual with representation theory, there is no free lunch. In the following, we will see the signature of the Hilbert-space curse of dimensionality in this picture, and explain how to side-step it by relaxing into a larger domain, L2​(SU​(2)N)L^{2}(\mathrm{SU}(2)^{N}), than the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} sector, while maintaining the variational principle, so that we can find ground-state energies of many-body systems.

First, though, let us build some intuition for the quaternionic representation, so that examples later in this part can be written directly in (q0,q1,q2,q3)(q_{0},q_{1},q_{2},q_{3}). Recall a unit quaternion q=(q0,q1,q2,q3)∈S3q=(q_{0},q_{1},q_{2},q_{3})\in S^{3} (q02+q12+q22+q32=1q_{0}^{2}+q_{1}^{2}+q_{2}^{2}+q_{3}^{2}=1) is the standard coordinate on SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) via

g⁡(q)=q0​I+qa​(i​σa)=(q0+i​q3q2+i​q1i​q1−q2q0−i​q3),g⁡(q)∈SU⁡(2),g(q)\;=\;q_{0}\,I+q_{a}\,(i\sigma^{a})\;=\;\begin{pmatrix}q_{0}+i\,q_{3}&q_{2}+i\,q_{1}\\[4.0pt] i\,q_{1}-q_{2}&q_{0}-i\,q_{3}\end{pmatrix},\qquad g(q)\in\mathrm{SU}(2), (S1.2)

where detg⁡(q)=q02+q12+q22+q32=1\det g(q)=q_{0}^{2}+q_{1}^{2}+q_{2}^{2}+q_{3}^{2}=1, and g⁡(q)​g​(q)†=Ig(q)\,g(q)^{\dagger}=I.

The four entries of g⁡(q)g(q) are the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} Wigner D-matrix elements. That is, for any spin jj, Dm​nj​(q)D^{j}_{mn}(q) is the matrix element of the rotation representation on the spin-jj irrep. For j=12j=\tfrac{1}{2} with row/column indices m,n∈{0,1}m,n\in\{0,1\},

Dm​n1/2​(q)=gm​n​(q),D001/2​(q)=q0+i​q3,D011/2​(q)=q2+i​q1,D101/2​(q)=i​q1−q2,D111/2​(q)=q0−i​q3.D^{1/2}_{mn}(q)\;=\;g_{mn}(q),\qquad\begin{array}[]{l}D^{1/2}_{00}(q)=q_{0}+i\,q_{3},\\[2.0pt] D^{1/2}_{01}(q)=q_{2}+i\,q_{1},\\[2.0pt] D^{1/2}_{10}(q)=i\,q_{1}-q_{2},\\[2.0pt] D^{1/2}_{11}(q)=q_{0}-i\,q_{3}.\end{array} (S1.3)

To identify physical single-site spin states with SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2)-functions, we fix the row m=0m=0, because the column index carries the physical spin. Thus

|↑⟩⟷D001/2​(q)=q0+i​q3,|↓⟩⟷D011/2​(q)=q2+i​q1.|\uparrow\rangle\longleftrightarrow D^{1/2}_{00}(q)=q_{0}+iq_{3},\qquad|\downarrow\rangle\longleftrightarrow D^{1/2}_{01}(q)=q_{2}+iq_{1}. (S1.4)

A general single-site state α​|↑⟩+β​|↓⟩\alpha|\!\uparrow\rangle+\beta|\!\downarrow\rangle becomes

ψ⁡(q)=α⁡(q0+i​q3)+β⁡(q2+i​q1).\psi(q)=\alpha(q_{0}+iq_{3})+\beta(q_{2}+iq_{1}). (S1.5)

For NN sites, let sk∈{0,1}s_{k}\in\{0,1\} with 0≡↑0\equiv\uparrow and 1≡↓1\equiv\downarrow. Then

|s1⋯sN⟩⟷∏k=1ND0,sk1/2(qk),|s_{1}\cdots s_{N}\rangle\longleftrightarrow\prod_{k=1}^{N}D^{1/2}_{0,s_{k}}(q_{k}), (S1.6)

and a general spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} state is a linear combination of these products; see SM § S1.3.

Recall a variational ansatz Ψθ\Psi_{\theta} over the physical Hilbert space (ℂ2)⊗N(\mathbb{C}^{2})^{\otimes N} gives an upper bound

⟨Ψθ|H|Ψθ⟩⟨Ψθ|Ψθ⟩≥E0\frac{\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\,H\,|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\,\Psi_{\theta}\rangle}\;\;\geq\;\;E_{0} (S1.7)

for any normalised Ψθ\Psi_{\theta}. Minimising this over θ\theta converges to (or above) E0E_{0}. This is the variational principle in its standard form, the rest of SM § S1 is about preserving this inequality under our non-standard quaternionic parameterisation.

We instantiate the manifold amplitude as a neural network returning

log⁡ψθ:SU​(2)N⟶ℂ.\log\psi_{\theta}:\mathrm{SU}(2)^{N}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}. (S1.8)

For the multilinear architecture, its Peter–Weyl coefficients carry a row-index multiplicity and a column-index physical-spin factor. Fixing a row multiplicity vector recovers the state-vector lift described above; a general model state is interpreted through the decomposition of Sec. S1.3.

We defer the details of the architecture to SM § S2, but the signature is a smooth non-linear function on the manifold, to be optimised by gradient descent on a variational loss. As is standard practise in Quantum Variational Monte Carlo, we use log⁡ψθ\log\psi_{\theta} to prevent underflow, and to allow for stable natural gradient flow [115].

Having now fixed our model to be a smooth 4​N4N-input, 11-output complex-valued network, predicting log⁡ψθ\log\psi_{\theta} on the Lie-group manifold, we can now turn to the question of how the Hamiltonian acts on this object, and how to project this object into the physical spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} sector of this function family.

S1.2 Operators with automatic differentiation

In this subsection we explain how the shift away from Hilbert space lets us realise the action of spin operators as Lie derivatives, executable directly through automatic differentiation. We restrict attention to quadratic, that is two-body, Hamiltonians throughout, since two-body interactions are universal for quantum [141], and higher-order interactions can be built from them [142, 143].

Recall from the standard theory that at each site ii, the spin is carried by three Hermitian operators S^ix,S^iy,S^iz\hat{S}_{i}^{x},\hat{S}_{i}^{y},\hat{S}_{i}^{z}, closing the algebra [S^ia,S^ib]=i​εa​b​c​S^ic[\hat{S}_{i}^{a},\hat{S}_{i}^{b}]=i\,\varepsilon_{abc}\,\hat{S}_{i}^{c}. Their squared magnitude is the Casimir S^i2:=(S^ix)2+(S^iy)2+(S^iz)2\hat{S}_{i}^{2}:=(\hat{S}_{i}^{x})^{2}+(\hat{S}_{i}^{y})^{2}+(\hat{S}_{i}^{z})^{2}, which on a single spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} is the scalar 34\tfrac{3}{4}, and we write σ^ia:=2​S^ia\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{a}:=2\,\hat{S}_{i}^{a} for the associated Pauli matrices. The most general quadratic Hamiltonian we target couples these Paulis pairwise, together with an on-site field,

H^=14​∑i<j∑a,bJi​ja​b​σ^ia​σ^jb+12​∑i,ahia​σ^ia,\hat{H}\;=\;\frac{1}{4}\!\sum_{i<j}\sum_{a,b}J_{ij}^{ab}\,\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{a}\,\hat{\sigma}_{j}^{b}\;+\;\frac{1}{2}\!\sum_{i,a}h_{i}^{a}\,\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{a}, (S1.9)

with exchange tensor J∈ℝN×N×3×3J\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times 3\times 3} and field h∈ℝN×3h\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}. As stated in the main text, it is useful to think of JJ as the data of a weighted interaction graph on NN sites, where each unordered pair (i,j)(i,j) with i≠ji\neq j carries a 3×33\times 3 Pauli-pair coupling matrix Ji​j∈ℝ3×3J_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}.

To move this operator onto the manifold, we use on the iith copy of SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) the left-invariant vector fields

(Lia​f)​(qi):=dd​t​f​(qi​exp⁡(t​Xa))|t=0,(L_{i}^{a}f)(q_{i}):=\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}f\!\left(q_{i}\exp(tX_{a})\right)\right|_{t=0}, (S1.10)

the anti-Hermitian infinitesimal generators of right translations. For Dm​nj​(q)=⟨j,m​|Dj​(q)|​j,n⟩D^{j}_{mn}(q)=\langle j,m|D^{j}(q)|j,n\rangle, they act on the column index:

Lia​Dm​nj​(qi)=∑rDm​rj​(qi)​(d​Dj​(Xa))r​n.L_{i}^{a}D^{j}_{mn}(q_{i})=\sum_{r}D^{j}_{mr}(q_{i})\,\bigl(\mathrm{d}D^{j}(X_{a})\bigr)_{rn}. (S1.11)

We therefore use the column index nn as the physical spin index and the row index mm as the Peter–Weyl multiplicity. The fields close [Lia,Lib]=κ​εa​b​c​Lic[L_{i}^{a},L_{i}^{b}]=\kappa\,\varepsilon_{abc}L_{i}^{c}, with κ=−2\kappa=-2 in the unit-length (half-Lie) normalisation we adopt. Setting S^ia=c​Lia\hat{S}_{i}^{a}=cL_{i}^{a} and matching the two algebras forces c​κ=ic\kappa=i, hence c=i/κ=−i2c=i/\kappa=-\tfrac{i}{2} and σ^ia=2​c​Lia=−i​Lia\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{a}=2cL_{i}^{a}=-iL_{i}^{a}.

Under this identification each Pauli pair becomes σ^ia​σ^jb=−Lia​Ljb\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{a}\hat{\sigma}_{j}^{b}=-L_{i}^{a}L_{j}^{b} and each field term becomes σ^ia=−i​Lia\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{a}=-i\,L_{i}^{a}, so the Hamiltonian (S1.9) turns into the second-order differential operator

H^↔−14∑i<j,a,bJi​ja​bLiaLjb−i2∑i,ahiaLia\hat{H}\;\leftrightarrow\;-\,\frac{1}{4}\!\sum_{i<j,a,b}J_{ij}^{ab}\,L_{i}^{a}L_{j}^{b}\;-\;\frac{i}{2}\!\sum_{i,a}h_{i}^{a}\,L_{i}^{a} (S1.12)

on L2​(SU​(2)N)L^{2}(\mathrm{SU}(2)^{N}). The same identification sends the spin magnitude to a Laplacian: S^i2=c2​∑a(Lia)2=−Δi\hat{S}_{i}^{2}=c^{2}\sum_{a}(L_{i}^{a})^{2}=-\Delta_{i}, where Δi:=14​∑a(Lia)2\Delta_{i}:=\tfrac{1}{4}\sum_{a}(L_{i}^{a})^{2} is the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the ii-th sphere.

What makes (S1.12) executable is that each LiaL_{i}^{a} is a known linear combination of the four partial derivatives ∂/∂qi,μ\partial/\partial q_{i,\mu} at site ii,

Lia=∑μ=03Aμa​(qi)​∂∂qi,μ,L_{i}^{a}\;=\;\sum_{\mu=0}^{3}A^{a}_{\mu}(q_{i})\;\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{i,\mu}}, (S1.13)

with coefficients AμaA^{a}_{\mu} the left-invariant frame on S3≅SU⁡(2)S^{3}\cong\mathrm{SU}(2), obtained by right-multiplying qiq_{i} by the three imaginary quaternion units ı^,ȷ^,k^\hat{\imath},\hat{\jmath},\hat{k},

[Aμx​(q)]μ=0,1,2,3\displaystyle\bigl[A^{x}_{\mu}(q)\bigr]_{\mu=0,1,2,3} =(−q3,q2,−q1,q0),\displaystyle=(-q_{3},\;q_{2},\;-q_{1},\;q_{0}), (S1.14)
[Aμy​(q)]\displaystyle\bigl[A^{y}_{\mu}(q)\bigr] =(−q2,−q3,q0,q1),\displaystyle=(-q_{2},\;-q_{3},\;q_{0},\;q_{1}),
[Aμz​(q)]\displaystyle\bigl[A^{z}_{\mu}(q)\bigr] =(−q1,q0,q3,−q2).\displaystyle=(-q_{1},\;q_{0},\;q_{3},\;-q_{2}).

A direct expansion using |q|2=1|q|^{2}=1 gives the identity we will lean on,

∑a∈{x,y,z}Aμa​(q)​Aνa​(q)=δμ​ν−qμ​qν=[PTq​S3]μ​ν,\sum_{a\in\{x,y,z\}}A^{a}_{\mu}(q)\,A^{a}_{\nu}(q)\;=\;\delta_{\mu\nu}-q_{\mu}q_{\nu}\;=\;\bigl[P_{T_{q}S^{3}}\bigr]_{\mu\nu}, (S1.15)

so the three tangents Aa​(q)A^{a}(q) are orthonormal and their outer product is the ambient projector onto Tq​S3T_{q}S^{3}. This is what makes {La}\{L^{a}\} a genuine orthonormal frame of the round metric, and hence Δi\Delta_{i} the Laplace–Beltrami operator named above. When two Lie derivatives act on the same site the channel sum (S1.15) applies; across two distinct sites the two frames carry different arguments and are simply transported along.

Equation (S1.13) makes the differential action computationally tractable. The custom forward-Laplacian propagates the value, the required first derivatives, and their contracted second derivatives together through one structured program traversal, never needing to materialise a dense Hessian. We can also avoid running an independent second-order pass for every pair. For a Hamiltonian with edge set ℰ\mathcal{E}, the pair contraction has leading combinatorial cost 𝒪⁡(|ℰ|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{E}|), which is 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) in the dense case. Here ℰ\mathcal{E} is the Hamiltonian’s interacting edge set. In the balanced readout, whose padded width is N^:=2⌈log2⁡N⌉\hat{N}:=2^{\lceil\log_{2}N\rceil}, the cross-derivative work summed over levels is likewise 𝒪⁡(N^2)\mathcal{O}(\hat{N}^{2}) with model-width factors suppressed. .

Applying the frame (S1.13) to the Lie form (S1.12) now gives the action of H^\hat{H} on ψ\psi in quaternionic coordinates. In a pair term the outer derivative LiaL_{i}^{a} meets the frame Ab​(qj)A^{b}(q_{j}) of the other site as a constant, so it contributes a pure second derivative with no first-order remainder, while the field term stays first order. Hence, for any Ji​ja​bJ_{ij}^{ab},

H^ψ(q)=−14∑i<j,a,bJi​ja​b∑μ,ν=03Aμa(qi)Aνb(qj)∂2ψ∂qi,μ​∂qj,ν(q)−i2∑i,ahia∑μAμa(qi)∂ψ∂qi,μ(q).\hat{H}\,\psi(q)\;=\;-\,\frac{1}{4}\!\sum_{i<j,a,b}\!J_{ij}^{ab}\!\sum_{\mu,\nu=0}^{3}\!A^{a}_{\mu}(q_{i})\,A^{b}_{\nu}(q_{j})\,\frac{\partial^{2}\psi}{\partial q_{i,\mu}\,\partial q_{j,\nu}}(q)\;-\;\frac{i}{2}\!\sum_{i,a}\!h^{a}_{i}\!\sum_{\mu}\!A^{a}_{\mu}(q_{i})\,\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial q_{i,\mu}}(q). (S1.16)

One step remains to make this usable. The network returns log⁡ψθ\log\psi_{\theta}, not ψθ\psi_{\theta}, whereas the local energy needs ratios Lia​Ljb​ψθ/ψθL_{i}^{a}L_{j}^{b}\,\psi_{\theta}/\psi_{\theta}. Writing ψ=elog⁡ψ\psi=e^{\log\psi} and applying the two first-order operators in turn bridges the two: for any twice-differentiable ψ≠0\psi\neq 0, we have that,

Lia​Ljb​ψψ=Lia​Ljb​log⁡ψ+(Lia​log⁡ψ)​(Ljb​log⁡ψ).\frac{L_{i}^{a}L_{j}^{b}\,\psi}{\psi}\;=\;L_{i}^{a}L_{j}^{b}\,\log\psi\;+\;\bigl(L_{i}^{a}\,\log\psi\bigr)\,\bigl(L_{j}^{b}\,\log\psi\bigr). (S1.17)

On a single site, summing the diagonal channels means the spin magnitude S^l2=−Δl\hat{S}_{l}^{2}=-\Delta_{l} reads,

−Δl​ψψ=−Δl​log⁡ψ−14​∑a(Lla​log⁡ψ)2.\frac{-\Delta_{l}\,\psi}{\psi}\;=\;-\,\Delta_{l}\,\log\psi\;-\;\tfrac{1}{4}\sum_{a}\bigl(L_{l}^{a}\,\log\psi\bigr)^{2}. (S1.18)

Both (S1.17) and (S1.18) depend only on log⁡ψθ\log\psi_{\theta} and its first two derivatives at the sampled point. These same quantities determine local estimators for observables containing at most two spin operators, including all two-point correlation functions. In (S1.16), the Hamiltonian enters through the coefficients Ji​ja​bJ_{ij}^{ab} and hiah_{i}^{a} that contract these derivatives. In particular, the nonzero pattern of JJ carries the interaction graph. The graph is therefore supplied as data to the same differential expression, rather than encoded in a lattice-specific rule. Changing the topology or system size changes the tensor entries and index ranges, and the form of the calculation remains identical aside from that.

S1.2.1 Three examples from the many-body literature

To make (S1.16) concrete, we read off three couplings that recur across the spin-model literature. The isotropic Heisenberg model H^X​X​X=J​∑⟨i​j⟩∑aS^ia​S^ja\hat{H}_{XXX}=J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\sum_{a}\hat{S}_{i}^{a}\hat{S}_{j}^{a} has Ji​ja​b=J​δa​bJ_{ij}^{ab}=J\,\delta^{ab} on each bond and no field; its Lie form is −J4∑⟨i​j⟩,aLiaLja-\tfrac{J}{4}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,a}L_{i}^{a}L_{j}^{a}, since S^ia​S^ja=c2​Lia​Lja=−14​Lia​Lja\hat{S}_{i}^{a}\hat{S}_{j}^{a}=c^{2}L_{i}^{a}L_{j}^{a}=-\tfrac{1}{4}L_{i}^{a}L_{j}^{a}, and (S1.16) collapses to a diagonal channel sum,

H^X​X​Xψ(q)=−J4∑⟨i​j⟩∑a∈{x,y,z}∑μ,ν=03Aμa(qi)Aνa(qj)∂2ψ∂qi,μ​∂qj,ν(q),\hat{H}_{XXX}\,\psi(q)\;=\;-\,\tfrac{J}{4}\!\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\!\sum_{a\in\{x,y,z\}}\sum_{\mu,\nu=0}^{3}A^{a}_{\mu}(q_{i})\,A^{a}_{\nu}(q_{j})\,\frac{\partial^{2}\psi}{\partial q_{i,\mu}\,\partial q_{j,\nu}}(q), (S1.19)

three mixed-site Hessian sandwiches per bond, one per Pauli channel. The Kitaev-Γ\Gamma coupling H^Γ=∑⟨i​j⟩Γi​j​(S^iy​S^jz+S^iz​S^jy)\hat{H}_{\Gamma}=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\Gamma_{ij}\,(\hat{S}_{i}^{y}\hat{S}_{j}^{z}+\hat{S}_{i}^{z}\hat{S}_{j}^{y}) is symmetric off-diagonal, Ji​jy​z=Ji​jz​y=Γi​jJ_{ij}^{yz}=J_{ij}^{zy}=\Gamma_{ij}, and pairs the two cross-channels,

H^Γψ(q)=−14∑⟨i​j⟩Γi​j∑μ,ν=03[Aμy(qi)Aνz(qj)+Aμz(qi)Aνy(qj)]∂2ψ∂qi,μ​∂qj,ν(q).\hat{H}_{\Gamma}\,\psi(q)\;=\;-\,\tfrac{1}{4}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\Gamma_{ij}\sum_{\mu,\nu=0}^{3}\bigl[\,A^{y}_{\mu}(q_{i})\,A^{z}_{\nu}(q_{j})+A^{z}_{\mu}(q_{i})\,A^{y}_{\nu}(q_{j})\,\bigr]\frac{\partial^{2}\psi}{\partial q_{i,\mu}\,\partial q_{j,\nu}}(q). (S1.20)

The Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya coupling H^DM=∑⟨i​j⟩D→i​j⋅(S→^i×S→^j)\hat{H}_{\mathrm{DM}}=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\vec{D}_{ij}\cdot(\hat{\vec{S}}_{i}\times\hat{\vec{S}}_{j}) is antisymmetric, Ji​jb​c=∑aDi​ja​εa​b​cJ_{ij}^{bc}=\sum_{a}D_{ij}^{a}\,\varepsilon^{abc}, and collecting its three channels into a cross product (well defined because LiaL_{i}^{a} and LjbL_{j}^{b} commute for i≠ji\neq j) gives

H^DMψ(q)=−14∑⟨i​j⟩∑μ,ν=03D→i​j⋅[A→μ(qi)×A→ν(qj)]∂2ψ∂qi,μ​∂qj,ν(q),\hat{H}_{\mathrm{DM}}\,\psi(q)\;=\;-\,\tfrac{1}{4}\!\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\!\sum_{\mu,\nu=0}^{3}\vec{D}_{ij}\cdot\bigl[\,\vec{A}_{\mu}(q_{i})\times\vec{A}_{\nu}(q_{j})\,\bigr]\,\frac{\partial^{2}\psi}{\partial q_{i,\mu}\,\partial q_{j,\nu}}(q), (S1.21)

with A→μ​(q):=(Aμx,Aμy,Aμz)​(q)\vec{A}_{\mu}(q):=(A^{x}_{\mu},A^{y}_{\mu},A^{z}_{\mu})(q) the frame sliced at fixed μ\mu. Here the bracket is antisymmetric under the joint swap (i,μ)↔(j,ν)(i,\mu)\leftrightarrow(j,\nu) while the mixed Hessian is symmetric, so a Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya term contributes nothing when both legs sit on one site: there is no on-site DMI, exactly as the antisymmetry Jb​c=−Jc​bJ^{bc}=-J^{cb} demands.

S1.3 Peter–Weyl decomposition and the spin-1/2 sector

Here we use the Peter–Weyl decomposition to identify the physical spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} sector inside L2​(SU​(2)N)L^{2}(\mathrm{SU}(2)^{N}). We will show that the multilinear manifold ansatz occupies a strictly larger ambient function class than a fixed lift of any NQS family, while the physical Hilbert space itself remains 2N2^{N}-dimensional. The comparison concerns ambient function classes; finite-parameter expressivity depends on the chosen architecture. We then establish the variational principle on the target spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} sector.

The Peter–Weyl theorem decomposes the single-site space into the matrix coefficients of the irreducible representations,

L2​(SU⁡(2))≅⨁j=0,12,1,32,…Vj∗⊗Vj.L^{2}\bigl(\mathrm{SU}(2)\bigr)\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{j=0,\tfrac{1}{2},1,\tfrac{3}{2},\dots}V_{j}^{*}\otimes V_{j}. (S1.22)

Here Dm​nj​(q)=⟨j,m​|Dj​(q)|​j,n⟩D^{j}_{mn}(q)=\langle j,m|D^{j}(q)|j,n\rangle carries the row index mm in the first, multiplicity factor Vj∗V_{j}^{*} and the column index nn in the second, physical factor VjV_{j}. The coefficients {Dm​nj}m,n=−j,…,j\{D^{j}_{mn}\}_{m,n=-j,\dots,j} form a complete orthogonal basis under the Haar measure, with ‖Dm​nj‖L22=1/(2​j+1)\|D^{j}_{mn}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=1/(2j+1). The spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} coefficients Dm​n1/2D^{1/2}_{mn} are the four entries of g⁡(q)g(q) from § S1.1; the higher-jj coefficients are the degree-2​j2j monomials in those entries.

On NN sites the basis is the product

Φ𝑱,𝒎,𝒏​(q1,…,qN)=∏k=1NDmk,nkjk​(qk),\Phi_{\boldsymbol{J},\boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{n}}(q_{1},\dots,q_{N})=\prod_{k=1}^{N}D^{j_{k}}_{m_{k},n_{k}}(q_{k}), (S1.23)

labelled by 𝑱=(j1,…,jN)\boldsymbol{J}=(j_{1},\dots,j_{N}), and the full space splits as

L2​(SU​(2)N)≅⨁𝑱⨂k=1N(Vjk∗⊗Vjk).L^{2}(\mathrm{SU}(2)^{N})\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{J}}\bigotimes_{k=1}^{N}\bigl(V_{j_{k}}^{*}\otimes V_{j_{k}}\bigr). (S1.24)

with Jk∈{0,12,1,…}J_{k}\in\{0,\tfrac{1}{2},1,\dots\}, and any ψ\psi has a unique expansion,

ψ=∑𝑱,𝒎,𝒏c𝑱,𝒎,𝒏​Φ𝑱,𝒎,𝒏.\psi=\sum_{\boldsymbol{J},\boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{n}}c_{\boldsymbol{J},\boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{n}}\,\Phi_{\boldsymbol{J},\boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{n}}. (S1.25)

The per-site Casimir of § S1.2 acts diagonally on this basis. Each Dm​njD^{j}_{mn} restricts to a degree-2​j2j harmonic polynomial in the quaternion coordinates, on which −Δi-\Delta_{i} carries the eigenvalue j⁡(j+1)j(j+1),

−Δi​Dmi,niji​(qi)=ji​(ji+1)​Dmi,niji​(qi),-\,\Delta_{i}\,D^{j_{i}}_{m_{i},n_{i}}(q_{i})\;=\;j_{i}(j_{i}+1)\,D^{j_{i}}_{m_{i},n_{i}}(q_{i}), (S1.26)

and in particular −Δi​Dm​n1/2=34​Dm​n1/2-\Delta_{i}\,D^{1/2}_{mn}=\tfrac{3}{4}\,D^{1/2}_{mn}, the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} value S^i2=34\hat{S}_{i}^{2}=\tfrac{3}{4} recorded in § S1.2.

The consequence for the network is immediate. An unconstrained ψθ∈L2​(SU​(2)N)\psi_{\theta}\in L^{2}(\mathrm{SU}(2)^{N}) generically has c𝑱,𝒎,𝒏≠0c_{\boldsymbol{J},\boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{n}}\neq 0 for every multi-index 𝑱\boldsymbol{J} in the expansion, integer and half-integer alike. It is not a spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} wavefunction, nor even a single-spin-jj wavefunction; its image lives across the full direct sum.

Indeed, the physical content occupies a single slice of that sum. A wavefunction ψ\psi describes NN genuine spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} degrees of freedom, one per site, precisely when it is an eigenfunction of every per-site Casimir at the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} value,

−Δk​ψ=34​ψfor every site ​k=1,…,N.-\,\Delta_{k}\,\psi\;=\;\tfrac{3}{4}\,\psi\qquad\text{for every site }k=1,\dots,N. (∗\ast)

Condition ( ∗ ‣ S1.3) selects the Peter–Weyl sector 𝑱=(12,…,12)\boldsymbol{J}=(\tfrac{1}{2},\dots,\tfrac{1}{2}), and projecting a generic manifold function onto it is what turns it into a physical state. This leads us to the following proposition.

Proposition S1.1 (The spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} sector).

A function ψ∈L2​(SU​(2)N)\psi\in L^{2}(\mathrm{SU}(2)^{N}) satisfies ( ∗ ‣ S1.3) if and only if

ψ⁡(q1,…,qN)=∑𝒎,𝒏T𝒎,𝒏​∏k=1NDmk,nk1/2​(qk),T𝒎,𝒏∈ℂ.\psi(q_{1},\dots,q_{N})\;=\;\sum_{\boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{n}}T_{\boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{n}}\,\prod_{k=1}^{N}D^{1/2}_{m_{k},n_{k}}(q_{k}),\qquad T_{\boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{n}}\in\mathbb{C}. (S1.27)

The coefficient tensor T∈ℂ4NT\in\mathbb{C}^{4^{N}} parameterises the entire sector. Fixing the fiducial row mk=0m_{k}=0 at every site fixes the Peter–Weyl multiplicity and leaves the 2N2^{N} coefficients indexed by 𝒏\boldsymbol{n}; these are the amplitudes of Ψ∈(ℂ2)⊗N\Psi\in(\mathbb{C}^{2})^{\otimes N} under the identification of § S1.1.

The proof, a term-by-term application of the Casimir eigen-equation (S1.26), is given in Appendix B.1.

To see how Prop. S1.1 works, it is instructive to write down some entangled states of interest to the quantum information community directly in the quaternionic coordinates of § S1.1.

The Bell state |Φ+⟩=12(|↑↑⟩+|↓↓⟩)|\Phi^{+}\rangle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|\!\uparrow\uparrow\rangle+|\!\downarrow\downarrow\rangle) and singlet |Ψ−⟩=12(|↑↓⟩−|↓↑⟩)|\Psi^{-}\rangle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|\!\uparrow\downarrow\rangle-|\!\downarrow\uparrow\rangle) read

ψΦ+​(q1,q2)\displaystyle\psi_{\Phi^{+}}(q_{1},q_{2}) =12​[(q1,0+i​q1,3)​(q2,0+i​q2,3)+(q1,2+i​q1,1)​(q2,2+i​q2,1)],\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\Bigl[(q_{1,0}+iq_{1,3})(q_{2,0}+iq_{2,3})+(q_{1,2}+iq_{1,1})(q_{2,2}+iq_{2,1})\Bigr],

The three-site GHZ and W states, which read,

|GHZ⟩\displaystyle|\mathrm{GHZ}\rangle =12(|↑↑↑⟩+|↓↓↓⟩),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|\!\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow\rangle+|\!\downarrow\downarrow\downarrow\rangle),
|W⟩\displaystyle|\mathrm{W}\rangle =13(|↑↑↓⟩+|↑↓↑⟩+|↓↑↑⟩),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(|\!\uparrow\uparrow\downarrow\rangle+|\!\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow\rangle+|\!\downarrow\uparrow\uparrow\rangle),

have manifold representatives,

ψGHZ​(q1,q2,q3)\displaystyle\psi_{\mathrm{GHZ}}(q_{1},q_{2},q_{3}) =12​[∏k=13(qk,0+i​qk,3)+∏k=13(qk,2+i​qk,1)],\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\Bigl[\textstyle\prod_{k=1}^{3}(q_{k,0}+iq_{k,3})+\prod_{k=1}^{3}(q_{k,2}+iq_{k,1})\Bigr],

+(q1,2+iq1,1)(q2,0+iq2,3)(q3,0+iq3,3)].\displaystyle\qquad\quad+(q_{1,2}+iq_{1,1})(q_{2,0}+iq_{2,3})(q_{3,0}+iq_{3,3})\Bigr].

Each state is a linear combination of products with the single fiducial row mk=0m_{k}=0, exactly the physical lift described above and the form allowed by Proposition S1.1.

We can now state the comparison with neural quantum states precisely. Let G=SU⁡(2)G=\mathrm{SU}(2) and define

𝒦N:=(V1/2∗)⊗N,ℋN:=V1/2⊗N,\mathcal{K}_{N}:=(V_{1/2}^{*})^{\otimes N},\qquad\mathcal{H}_{N}:=V_{1/2}^{\otimes N}, (S1.28)

where 𝒦N\mathcal{K}_{N} carries the row/multiplicity indices 𝒎\boldsymbol{m} and ℋN\mathcal{H}_{N} carries the column/physical indices 𝒏\boldsymbol{n}. The multilinear and per-site-odd function spaces are

ℱlin\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{lin}} :=span⁡{∏i=1NDmi​ni1/2​(qi)}≅𝒦N⊗ℋN,\displaystyle:=\operatorname{span}\!\left\{\prod_{i=1}^{N}D^{1/2}_{m_{i}n_{i}}(q_{i})\right\}\cong\mathcal{K}_{N}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{N}, (S1.29)
ℱodd\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{odd}} :={f∈L2(GN):f(…,−qi,…)=−f(…,qi,…)∀i}\displaystyle:=\left\{f\in L^{2}(G^{N}):f(\ldots,-q_{i},\ldots)=-f(\ldots,q_{i},\ldots)\ \forall i\right\}
=⨁j1,…,jN∈{12,32,…}⨂i=1N(Vji∗⊗Vji).\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{j_{1},\ldots,j_{N}\in\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\ldots\}}\bigotimes_{i=1}^{N}\bigl(V_{j_{i}}^{*}\otimes V_{j_{i}}\bigr). (S1.30)

Fix any unit vector χ∈𝒦N\chi\in\mathcal{K}_{N}. Its canonical lift is

ιχ​(Ψ)​(q1,…,qN):=2N/2​∑𝒎,𝒏χ𝒎​Ψ𝒏​∏i=1NDmi​ni1/2​(qi).\iota_{\chi}(\Psi)(q_{1},\ldots,q_{N}):=2^{N/2}\!\sum_{\boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{n}}\chi_{\boldsymbol{m}}\Psi_{\boldsymbol{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{N}D^{1/2}_{m_{i}n_{i}}(q_{i}). (S1.31)
Theorem S1.2 (Ambient expressivity hierarchy).

For N≥1N\geq 1, the lift (S1.31) is an isometry and

ιχ​(ℋN)⊊ℱlin⊊ℱodd.\iota_{\chi}(\mathcal{H}_{N})\;\subsetneq\;\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{lin}}\;\subsetneq\;\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{odd}}. (S1.32)

Consequently, for every NQS variational family ℳNQS⊆ℋN\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{NQS}}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{N},

ιχ​(ℳNQS)⊆ιχ​(ℋN)⊊ℱlin⊊ℱodd.\iota_{\chi}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{NQS}})\;\subseteq\;\iota_{\chi}(\mathcal{H}_{N})\;\subsetneq\;\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{lin}}\;\subsetneq\;\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{odd}}. (S1.33)

Let H~\widetilde{H} be the right-regular differential representation of the physical Hamiltonian HH, generated by the left-invariant fields. On the linear class,

H~|ℱlin≅I𝒦N⊗HℋN,\widetilde{H}\big|_{\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{lin}}}\cong I_{\mathcal{K}_{N}}\otimes H_{\mathcal{H}_{N}}, (S1.34)

where HℋNH_{\mathcal{H}_{N}} denotes HH acting on ℋN\mathcal{H}_{N}. Consequently, every nonzero f∈ℱlinf\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{lin}} obeys

⟨f,H~​f⟩⟨f,f⟩≥E0,inff∈ℱlin∖{0}⟨f,H~​f⟩⟨f,f⟩=E0.\frac{\langle f,\widetilde{H}f\rangle}{\langle f,f\rangle}\geq E_{0},\qquad\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{lin}}\setminus\{0\}}\frac{\langle f,\widetilde{H}f\rangle}{\langle f,f\rangle}=E_{0}. (S1.35)

C^:=∑i=1N(S^i2−34​I).\widehat{C}:=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\widehat{S}_{i}^{2}-\frac{3}{4}I\right). (S1.36)

⟨f,(H~+λ​C^)​f⟩⟨f,f⟩≥E0for all ​f∈ℱodd∖{0},\frac{\langle f,(\widetilde{H}+\lambda\widehat{C})f\rangle}{\langle f,f\rangle}\geq E_{0}\quad\text{for all }f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{odd}}\setminus\{0\}, (S1.37)

and the infimum of the regularised quotient over ℱodd∖{0}\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{odd}}\setminus\{0\} is exactly E0E_{0}.

The strict containments in Theorem S1.2 concern functions on the group manifold. The additional row Peter–Weyl index is a multiplicity, or purification, degree of freedom on which the physical Hamiltonian acts trivially; the column index carries the physical spin. This does not enlarge the physical 2N2^{N}-dimensional Hilbert space. Likewise, the nonlinear class adds higher-half-integer sectors that become variationally consistent only after the Casimir penalty. The theorem proves the exact ambient hierarchy and the variational principle for both the linear and nonlinear cases.

S1.4 Central oddness and variational principles

Notice first that the Peter–Weyl expansion splits into two parity classes under the per-site reflection qi→−qiq_{i}\to-q_{i}. The point −q-q represents the central element −I∈SU⁡(2)-I\in\mathrm{SU}(2), which acts on the spin-jj irrep as the scalar (−1)2​j(-1)^{2j}, so the Wigner coefficients carry that same sign,

Dm​nj​(−q)=(−1)2​j​Dm​nj​(q),D^{j}_{mn}(-q)\;=\;(-1)^{2j}\,D^{j}_{mn}(q), (S1.38)

even (+1+1) on the integer sectors and odd (−1-1) on the half-integer ones. The integer-jj sectors are therefore exactly the even subspace of L2​(SU​(2))L^{2}(\mathrm{SU}(2)), and the half-integer sectors the odd subspace.

Hence, per-site oddness,

ψ⁡(…,−qi,…)=−ψ⁡(…,qi,…)for every site ​i,\psi(\dots,-q_{i},\dots)\;=\;-\,\psi(\dots,q_{i},\dots)\qquad\text{for every site }i, (S1.39)

annihilates by (S1.38) every component with integer jij_{i}, and the support collapses onto the half-integer sectors ji∈{12,32,52,…}j_{i}\in\{\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{3}{2},\tfrac{5}{2},\dots\}, with the physical target ji=12j_{i}=\tfrac{1}{2} now the lowest of them.

The architecture of SM § S2 enforces (S1.39) exactly, so we take it as given here. Although each normalised carrier is a nonlinear function of its quaternion, the leaf and merge log-scales cancel those normalisations exactly in the reconstructed amplitude. Lemma S2.1 therefore shows that the final ψθ\psi_{\theta} is degree one in every qiq_{i}. A degree-one function on SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) is a linear combination of the four coefficients Dm​n1/2D^{1/2}_{mn}, so Proposition S1.1 places the ansatz in ℱlin\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{lin}} identically.

Two distinct cases follow as a consequence of Theorem S1.2. First, the foundation architecture we describe next is linear in each quaternion, so lies in ℱlin\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{lin}} and directly obeys the variational principle E⁡[ψθ]≥E0E[\psi_{\theta}]\geq E_{0}. Second, any future generation of model which is per-site odd but non-linear in the quaternioncs lies in the larger ℱodd\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{odd}}. Such a model’s higher-half-integeter sectors invalidate the variational principle as it stands, however it can be restored with an energy penalty restores the upper bound while retaining that larger ambient function class, see Appendix A.

S1.5 A topological obstruction to wavefunction-valued foundation models

In this subsection, we show that continuous pure-state foundation NQS cannot uniformly represent topologically nontrivial ground-state families. Theorem S1.2 already separates the ambient function classes at fixed Hamiltonian. The separation here is of a different kind and appears only at the level of a family of topologically distinct interacting Hamiltonians, where one set of model weights must serve every Hamiltonian of a this family at once.

Let XX be a compact manifold and H:X→Herm⁡(ℋN)H:X\to\mathrm{Herm}(\mathcal{H}_{N}) a continuous family with a nondegenerate ground state at every x∈Xx\in X. Compactness gives a uniform gap Δ:=minx∈X⁡[E1​(x)−E0​(x)]>0\Delta:=\min_{x\in X}\,[E_{1}(x)-E_{0}(x)]>0, and the ground-state projector P0​(x)P_{0}(x), the Riesz integral of the resolvent around E0​(x)E_{0}(x), is norm-continuous in xx [144]. Its range L:=Ran⁡P0⊂X×ℋNL:=\operatorname{Ran}P_{0}\subset X\times\mathcal{H}_{N} is therefore a complex line bundle over XX, the Berry bundle of the family [145, 146], classified up to isomorphism by its first Chern class c1​(L)∈H2​(X,ℤ)c_{1}(L)\in H^{2}(X;\mathbb{Z}).

A wavefunction-valued foundation model evaluated across the family is a continuous map Φ:X→ℋN∖{0}\Phi:X\to\mathcal{H}_{N}\setminus\{0\}, where the network reads the interaction data (J,h)(J,h) at xx and returns basis amplitudes. Hence, we can create a full state vector of basis amplitudes from this object, which is the form of the FNQS programme [22, 23]. The following theorem shows that a continuous family of Hamiltonians create a situation where a pure-state (wavefunction-valued) FNQS projection onto the ground state eigenspace is necessarily vanishing, creating a topological no-go theorem for such foundation models.

Theorem S1.3 (Topological no-go).

Let XX, HH, Δ\Delta, LL be as above with c1​(L)≠0c_{1}(L)\neq 0. Then every continuous Φ:X→ℋN∖{0}\Phi:X\to\mathcal{H}_{N}\setminus\{0\} satisfies P0​(x⋆)​Φ​(x⋆)=0P_{0}(x_{\star})\,\Phi(x_{\star})=0 at some x⋆∈Xx_{\star}\in X. Consequently

‖P0​(x⋆)​Φ​(x⋆)‖2‖Φ⁡(x⋆)‖2= 0and⟨Φ⁡(x⋆),H⁡(x⋆)​Φ​(x⋆)⟩⟨Φ⁡(x⋆),Φ⁡(x⋆)⟩≥E0​(x⋆)+Δ,\frac{\|P_{0}(x_{\star})\Phi(x_{\star})\|^{2}}{\|\Phi(x_{\star})\|^{2}}\;=\;0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{\langle\Phi(x_{\star}),\,H(x_{\star})\,\Phi(x_{\star})\rangle}{\langle\Phi(x_{\star}),\,\Phi(x_{\star})\rangle}\;\geq\;E_{0}(x_{\star})+\Delta, (S1.40)

so the worst-case ground-state fidelity of Φ\Phi over the family is zero and its worst-case energy error is at least one full gap inside XX.

Proof.

s⁡(x):=P0​(x)​Φ​(x)s(x):=P_{0}(x)\Phi(x) is a continuous section of LL. If ss vanished nowhere, x↦s⁡(x)/‖s⁡(x)‖x\mapsto s(x)/\|s(x)\| would be a global unit frame and LL would be trivial, contradicting c1​(L)≠0c_{1}(L)\neq 0. Hence s⁡(x⋆)=0s(x_{\star})=0 at some x⋆x_{\star}, i.e. Φ⁡(x⋆)∈Ran⁡(I−P0​(x⋆))\Phi(x_{\star})\in\operatorname{Ran}\,(I-P_{0}(x_{\star})), on which the Rayleigh quotient of H⁡(x⋆)H(x_{\star}) is at least E1​(x⋆)≥E0​(x⋆)+ΔE_{1}(x_{\star})\geq E_{0}(x_{\star})+\Delta. ∎

This theorem affects the zero-shot regime a foundation model. Per-instance fine-tuning evades it only by replacing the single map Φ\Phi with a different model for each Hamiltonian, which renders null the amortisation the foundation setting exists for. We can see this with the following one-qubit system example.

For H(n)=−∑anaσ^aH(n)=-\sum_{a}n^{a}\hat{\sigma}^{a} with n∈S2n\in S^{2}, the Berry bundle is the Hopf line bundle and |c1​(L)|=1|c_{1}(L)|=1 [145]. Every continuous Φ:S2→ℂ2∖{0}\Phi:S^{2}\to\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus\{0\} therefore returns the excited ray at some n⋆n_{\star}, with energy error 22, the full spectral width. The family embeds at any qubit number with fixed spectators,

HN(n)=−∑anaσ^1a−∑i=2Nσ^iz,H_{N}(n)\;=\;-\sum_{a}n^{a}\hat{\sigma}_{1}^{a}\;-\;\sum_{i=2}^{N}\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}, (S1.41)

whose ground state is nondegenerate with uniform gap 22 and whose Berry bundle is the Hopf line tensored with a trivial spectator line, so c1​(L)≠0c_{1}(L)\neq 0 persists. Single-site fields are part of the interaction data (J,h)(J,h) a foundation model must accept, so this obstructed two-sphere already lies inside the input class of any FNQS.

Because of this, the fidelity with true ground state will always vanish somewhere in XX when the wavefunction goes orthogonal to the true ground state. This can be especially misleading when using foundation models to sweep over phase diagrams, and would a false prediction of a phase transition.

Indeed, the ground-ray map g:X→ℙ⁡(ℋN)g:X\to\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{H}_{N}), x↦[Ψ0​(x)]x\mapsto[\Psi_{0}(x)], is globally continuous. A wavefunction-valued model attempts to recover a continuous lift g~:X→S⁡(ℋN)\widetilde{g}:X\to S(\mathcal{H}_{N}) of gg through the Hopf quotient π:S⁡(ℋN)→ℙ⁡(ℋN)\pi:S(\mathcal{H}_{N})\to\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{H}_{N}) from the unit sphere S⁡(ℋN)⊂ℋNS(\mathcal{H}_{N})\subset\mathcal{H}_{N}, and such a lift exists if and only if the pullback of the tautological line bundle, g∗​𝒪​(−1)≅Lg^{*}\mathcal{O}(-1)\cong L, is trivial [146]. Contrary to that, models like Hamilton-Zero are actually operator-valued and ℙ⁡(ℋN)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{H}_{N}) embed continuously in ℋN∗⊗ℋN=𝒦N⊗ℋN\mathcal{H}_{N}^{*}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{N}=\mathcal{K}_{N}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{N} by [Ψ]↦|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|[\Psi]\mapsto|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|, and x↦P0​(x)x\mapsto P_{0}(x) stays continuous whereas no continuous Ψ0\Psi_{0} exists. To elaborate on that, we note that ℋN∗⊗ℋN=End⁡(ℋN)\mathcal{H}_{N}^{*}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{N}=\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{H}_{N}) is a space of operators, which contain as a subspace a space of density operators. This is otherwise known as purification [147]. We also want to emphasize that this is distinct from router’s density mixture, and holds for its fixed permutation setting as well.

On degenerate ground-state manifolds, a kk-fold degenerate ground-state space defines a rank-kk Berry bundle with non-abelian holonomy [148]. Wavefunction-valued models then require continuous frames, obstructed by its characteristic classes beginning with the Euler class ckc_{k}. A systematic account of which Hamiltonian families are obstructed, and of what operator-valued ansätze can represent uniformly, is deferred to a forthcoming work.

Finally, we note that the bare existence of such cases is a no go for any globally defined foundation NQS in a setting that we operate in: arbitrary quadratic hamiltonian. We also note that this no-go applies should we have chosen a phase space like that of [40], since S2S^{2} suffers the same lifting problem whenever such a foundation-model is wavefunction-valued, and thus acting on only one component of the Peter-Weyl sector. We also note that doubling the number of binary variables would circumvent such an issue for the NQS community, as it makes an effective density matrix that can act on both components of the Peter-Weyl sector.

S2 Foundation Ansatz and Entanglement Structure via Reinforcement Learning

In this section, we describe the foundation model’s architecture. The model has two different types of input. First is the Hamiltonian’s interaction tensor (J,h)(J,h), and second is a spin configuration q∈S​U​(2)Nq\in SU(2)^{N} sampled from the model’s own density. In this section, we will assume efficient access to such samples, deferring the details of our novel sampling scheme to SM § S4.1.

These two sources of data naturally divide the architecture into two components that together allow us to simultaneously condition the foundation model wavefunction on the Hamiltonian (allowing for generalisation) as well as preserving the necessary exchange anti-symmetry of our quaternionic representation from SM § S1.

The first component, which we call the trunk, is a function of the Hamiltonian’s interaction tensor. In (§ S2.1) we describe how a given input (J,h)(J,h) is cached into two tensors J′′J^{\prime\prime} and h′′h^{\prime\prime}. In (§ S2.2) we then describe our learnable featurizer, which converts the cached inputs J′′J^{\prime\prime} and h′′h^{\prime\prime} into embeddings of the Hamiltonian’s system context for the trunk. We then describe the architecture of the trunk itself in (§ S2.3), which consists of LL residual attention blocks nested between feed-forward networks, as well as a per-site leaf builder where the spin configuration qq enters (§ S2.3).

The second component is a readout contraction mechanism of the trunk that incorporates spin coordinates. This component is akin to a tree-tensor network, augmented by three routines that enable generalisation to arbitrary quadratic Hamiltonians and system sizes. First, we use edge-level attention in a tree to enable it to condition on the Hamiltonian’s interaction tensor. Second, we use a learnable routing policy to allow the tree to entangle arbitrary sites in the system. Finally, we use a contextualizer to allow the tree to condition on Hamiltonian data while preserving the necessary exchange anti-symmetry of our quaternionic representation.

The contraction itself is detailed in (§ S2.4), where we describe a rank-4 quadrilinear merge with level attention on each contraction layer, as well as the contextualizer. Section (§ S2.5) then describes the learnable routing policy to optimise over contraction paths with deep reinforcement learning.

Together, the merged contraction with a learnable path enables arbitrary entanglement between sites, with the entanglement conditioned on the Hamiltonian’s interaction tensor (J,h)(J,h) enabling a Hamiltonian-dependent contraction pathway.

Figure S1 shows the information flow of our ansatz over a forward pass. Recall for the spin-configuration input q∈(SU⁡(2))Nq\in(\mathrm{SU}(2))^{N}, we use the quaternion representation embedded in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}, so qi=(qi,0,qi,1,qi,2,qi,3)q_{i}=(q_{i,0},q_{i,1},q_{i,2},q_{i,3}) with qi,02+qi,12+qi,22+qi,32=1q_{i,0}^{2}+q_{i,1}^{2}+q_{i,2}^{2}+q_{i,3}^{2}=1. This makes the input space a product of spheres SU⁡(2)≅S3↪ℝ4\mathrm{SU}(2)\cong S^{3}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{4}.

S2.1 Hamiltonian encoding and spectral normalisation

Recall from §S1.2 that the Hamiltonian family we target is

H^=14​∑i<j∑a,kJi​ja​k​σia​σjk+12​∑i∑ahia​σia,\hat{H}\;=\;\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i<j}\sum_{a,k}J^{ak}_{ij}\,\sigma^{a}_{i}\,\sigma^{k}_{j}\;+\;\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\sum_{a}h^{a}_{i}\,\sigma^{a}_{i}, (S2.1)

with exchange tensor J∈ℝN×N×3×3J\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times 3\times 3} (cross-channel Pauli-pair couplings on off-diagonal (i,j)(i,j)) and transverse field h∈ℝN×3h\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3} (per-site three-vector).

As stated in the main text, it is useful to think of JJ as the data of a weighted graph on NN sites, where each unordered pair (i,j)(i,j) with i≠ji\neq j carries a 3×33\times 3 Pauli-pair coupling matrix Ji​j∈ℝ3×3J_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}, which we read as nine flavours of edge, one per Pauli-pair (a,b)∈{x,y,z}2(a,b)\in\{x,y,z\}^{2} giving the operator σia​σjb\sigma^{a}_{i}\sigma^{b}_{j}, see Fig. 2.

We keep exchange and field as separate input channels for the model. Before feeding them into the model, we normalize them in the following way.

Step 1 (off-diagonal — bond-symmetrise).  On Hermitian-conjugate pairs (i,j)↔(j,i)(i,j)\leftrightarrow(j,i), average to enforce the swap symmetry:

Ji​j,a​bsym=12​(Ji​j,a​b+Jj​i,b​a∗)(i≠j).J^{\text{sym}}_{ij,ab}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\bigl(J_{ij,ab}+J^{*}_{ji,ba}\bigr)\qquad(i\neq j). (S2.2)

We do this because Pauli interactions are hermitian, so at the level of the interaction tensor and its relation to an interaction graph, it must be bi-directionally symmetric.

Step 2 (form the common Hermitian scale matrix).  For the scale computation only, the cache builder forms

Mi​j,a​b=Ji​j,a​bsym+δi​j​i​εa​b​c​hic,M_{ij,ab}\;=\;J^{\mathrm{sym}}_{ij,ab}+\delta_{ij}\,i\,\varepsilon_{abc}\,h_{i}^{c}, (S2.3)

and reshapes it as

M~:=reshape⁡(M, 3​N×3​N).\widetilde{M}:=\operatorname{reshape}(M,\,3N\times 3N). (S2.4)

For real hih_{i}, the block Ai,a​b:=εa​b​c​hicA_{i,ab}:=\varepsilon_{abc}h_{i}^{c} is real and antisymmetric, so

(i​Ai)†=i​Ai.(iA_{i})^{\dagger}=iA_{i}. (S2.5)

Together with the Hermitian swap symmetrisation of Step 1, this makes M~\widetilde{M} Hermitian. Its eigenvalues are therefore real, and the shared scale is

s:=‖M~‖2=maxk⁡|λk​(M~)|,s:=\|\widetilde{M}\|_{2}=\max_{k}\bigl|\lambda_{k}(\widetilde{M})\bigr|, (S2.6)

computed once per system with jnp.linalg.eigvalsh. The spectral radius maxk⁡|λk|\max_{k}|\lambda_{k}| is defined for every square matrix. The role of the factor ii is instead to make M~\widetilde{M} Hermitian, so that the Hermitian eigensolver is appropriate and the spectral radius equals the spectral norm. The diagonal field block participates only in this scale computation and is discarded afterwards.

Step 3 (normalise and flatten).  We divide the separate exchange and field channels by the same scale ss. The exchange keeps its off-diagonal bonds and an identity-marker channel, with the diagonal Pauli block left empty since the field no longer lives there,

Ji​j,c′′={(Jsym/s)i​j,a​b​(c)c=0,…,8​and​i≠j,0c=0,…,8​and​i=j,δi​jc=9,J^{\prime\prime}_{ij,c}\;=\;\begin{cases}(J^{\text{sym}}/s)_{ij,ab(c)}&c=0,\dots,8\ \text{and}\ i\neq j,\\ 0&c=0,\dots,8\ \text{and}\ i=j,\\ \delta_{ij}&c=9,\end{cases} (S2.7)

where c=0,…,8c=0,\dots,8 enumerates the nine (a,b)(a,b) pairs in row-major order, and the field is cached as its own per-site tensor,

hi′′=hi/s.h^{\prime\prime}_{i}\;=\;h_{i}/s. (S2.8)

Building these inputs costs one call to eigvalsh per system, paid once per system when a panel or an augmentation round is loaded, and once per system at evaluation or fine-tuning. We emphasise here that the size of the interaction tensor, and the graph that follows, is polynomial in the number of bodies, since our foundation model handles quadratic interactions which are a small sub-group of the overall Pauli group on NN spins.

By construction, this normalisation makes both cached inputs invariant under simultaneous rescaling (J,h)→α⁡(J,h)(J,h)\to\alpha(J,h) for α>0\alpha>0, since the spectral radius ss scales linearly with α\alpha. This avoids the attention layers needing to learn the invariance from our datasets. Under α<0\alpha<0 the inputs are sign-flip-equivariant: a global sign passes through to the nine Pauli channels of J′′J^{\prime\prime} and to h′′h^{\prime\prime}, while the identity channel is unaffected. Finally they are smooth at h=0h=0, since h′′h^{\prime\prime} is linear in hh and the scale ss stays bounded away from zero. These three properties are exactly the ones our featurizer (§ S2.2) relies on for equivariance under rescaling and for the h→0h\to 0 limit.

This encoding is a bijection between the original (J,h)(J,h) and the cached pair (J′′,h′′)(J^{\prime\prime},h^{\prime\prime}), and both representations are in the datasets we have open-sourced.

The diagonal field block in MM is solely a common-normalisation device. It is neither a cached model input nor a replacement of the physical first-order field operator. Including both exchange and field in M~\widetilde{M} lets one scale normalise the two channels together. Once ss has been computed, the diagonal block is discarded, and the model receives the bond tensor J′′J^{\prime\prime} and the per-site field h′′h^{\prime\prime} separately, while the local-energy expression retains the field as the first-order term in Eq. (S1.16).

The per-system rescaling-invariance is then the standard ML input-normalisation trick applied at the level of the Hamiltonian itself. Dividing through by the spectral radius lands every system in a unit-norm regime regardless of physical units, so the training dataset’s overall energy scale stops being a feature the network has to re-learn for every batch. Indeed this has direct analogy to dividing pixel values by 255255 or attention keys by d\sqrt{d}, removing a known-uninformative scale so the network spends capacity on what actually distinguishes systems. We can simply rescale the output by the renormalisation factor ss to get back to physical units, and optimise in the normalised space where the network is more stable and generalises better.

S2.2 Learnable featurizer

The featurizer is a single fusion block that consumes the two cached inputs and emits three downstream-ready tensors:

SystemFeaturizer:(J′′∈ℝN×N×10,h′′∈ℝN×3)⟼(e∈ℝN×N×96,ℓ∈ℝN×128,g∈ℝ1024).\texttt{SystemFeaturizer}:\;\bigl(\,J^{\prime\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times 10},\;h^{\prime\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}\,\bigr)\;\longmapsto\;\bigl(\;e\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times 96},\;\;\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 128},\;\;g\in\mathbb{R}^{1024}\;\bigr). (S2.9)

These three objects correspond to a per-bond embedding ee for the trunk’s attention layers, a per-site local embedding ℓ\ell for the trunk’s attention layers, and a global context vector gg that seeds the global stream the trunk maintains (§ S2.3). The featurizer is a single-pass architecture with no iteration or recurrence; it is a single function of the Hamiltonian that produces these three tensors in one go. Figure S2 shows the data-flow and we detail each step below.

Both cached tensors enter in polar form. We read the nine Pauli-pair entries of each bond block as a vector xi​jJ=vec(Ji​j,1:9′′)∈ℝ9x^{J}_{ij}=\mathrm{vec}(J^{\prime\prime}_{ij,1:9})\in\mathbb{R}^{9} and split it into a radius and a softened direction,

ri​jJ=∥xi​jJ∥2,ui​jJ=xi​jJ∥xi​jJ∥22+τ2,r^{J}_{ij}=\lVert x^{J}_{ij}\rVert_{2},\qquad u^{J}_{ij}=\frac{x^{J}_{ij}}{\sqrt{\lVert x^{J}_{ij}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\tau^{2}}}, (S2.10)

where τ=10−3\tau=10^{-3} is a fixed feature-scale floor, and ||⋅||2||\cdot||_{2} is the Euclidean norm. The radius rJr^{J} shows whether a bond is present, whilst the direction uJu^{J} reports its angular type and stays bounded as the bond vanishes. Notice τ\tau is a fixed feature-scale floor, not a numerical ε\varepsilon. The bond input stacks the raw, radial, angular, and self-bond coordinates, and the field is lifted the same way,

x^i​jJ=[xi​jJ,ri​jJ,ui​jJ, 1i=j]∈ℝ20,x^ih=[hi′′,∥hi′′∥2,hi′′∥hi′′∥22+τ2]∈ℝ7.\hat{x}^{J}_{ij}=\bigl[\,x^{J}_{ij},\;r^{J}_{ij},\;u^{J}_{ij},\;\mathbf{1}_{i=j}\,\bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{20},\qquad\hat{x}^{h}_{i}=\Bigl[\,h^{\prime\prime}_{i},\;\lVert h^{\prime\prime}_{i}\rVert_{2},\;\tfrac{h^{\prime\prime}_{i}}{\sqrt{\lVert h^{\prime\prime}_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\tau^{2}}}\,\Bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{7}. (S2.11)

They are functions of the cached inputs alone and are computed once per system alongside them (§ S2.1). We hand the model the coordinate, its magnitude, and its direction separately rather than make a dense layer recover all three: the loci that matter physically, vanishing bonds or fields, isotropic blocks, vanishing skew or symmetric-traceless parts, rank-deficient couplings, are exactly where a plain projection smears presence into direction.

The two embedding paths normalise in groups, and the normalisation is the root-mean-square kind throughout: for a vector zz with learned per-channel scale γ\gamma,

RMS⁡(z)=γ⊙zz2¯+ε,z2¯:=1d​∑aza2,\mathrm{RMS}(z)\;=\;\gamma\odot\frac{z}{\sqrt{\overline{z^{2}}+\varepsilon}},\qquad\overline{z^{2}}\;:=\;\tfrac{1}{d}\textstyle\sum_{a}z_{a}^{2}, (S2.12)

with no mean subtraction and no shift. The mean subtraction of LayerNorm is left out on purpose: it couples every channel through a shared offset and worsens the conditioning of the curvature the optimiser preconditions against, and dropping it is the same trade that moved the large-language-model community from LayerNorm to RMSNorm [149]. Every normalisation layer on the even path, here and in every later stage, is of this form. Reshaping a vector into KK groups of width dgrpd_{\mathrm{grp}}, the grouped variant normalises each group on its own with its own scale,

GRMS​(z)k=γk​zkzk2¯+ε,γk=𝟏​at init,\mathrm{GRMS}(z)_{k}=\gamma_{k}\,\frac{z_{k}}{\sqrt{\overline{z_{k}^{2}}+\varepsilon}},\qquad\gamma_{k}=\mathbf{1}\;\text{at init}, (S2.13)

with zk2¯\overline{z_{k}^{2}} the mean square within group kk. Each group is then free to become a learned filter over the raw, radial, and angular coordinates, a data-driven stand-in for the named decomposition J=t​I+Q+AJ=tI+Q+A into isotropic, symmetric-traceless, and skew parts, without hard-coding it. We use K=16K=16 groups of width dgrp=16d_{\mathrm{grp}}=16 on both paths.

The per-bond embedding is then a two-layer map, a grouped norm, and two more layers,

zi​jJ=GRMS⁡(SiLU⁡(x^i​jJ​W1J)​W2J),Bi​j=mi​mj⋅SiLU⁡(SiLU⁡(zi​jJ​W3J)​W4J),z^{J}_{ij}=\mathrm{GRMS}\!\bigl(\mathrm{SiLU}(\hat{x}^{J}_{ij}\,W^{J}_{1})\,W^{J}_{2}\bigr),\qquad B_{ij}=m_{i}m_{j}\cdot\mathrm{SiLU}\!\bigl(\mathrm{SiLU}(z^{J}_{ij}\,W^{J}_{3})\,W^{J}_{4}\bigr), (S2.14)

with dbond=128d_{\text{bond}}=128, every bias zero at initialisation, and mi​mjm_{i}m_{j} the site-padding pair mask: it zeroes pairs with a padded endpoint and carries no bond information.

Bonds absent from the system’s adjacency pattern are not masked to zero. Wherever a bond feature is consumed, absence substitutes a learned token in its place,

zi​j⟵{zi​j,presenti​jt,otherwisepresenti​j=[∃c≤8:Ji​j,c′′≠0]∨[i=j],z_{ij}\;\longleftarrow\;\begin{cases}z_{ij},&\mathrm{present}_{ij}\\ t,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\qquad\mathrm{present}_{ij}\;=\;\bigl[\,\exists\,c\leq 8:\;J^{\prime\prime}_{ij,c}\neq 0\,\bigr]\;\vee\;[\,i=j\,], (S2.15)

with one trained token tt per consumption site. Six sites carry a token: the bond embedding, the bond attention’s key and value input, the Zeeman base, the field’s row-attention view, the field branch of the global fusion, and the field’s entry in the local cross-conditioning. On the field path a zero field substitutes its tokens the same way, per site everywhere except the fusion branch, which gates per system. The physical reading is that “no bond” becomes a representable direction of the basis rather than the numeric zero, while the substitution still cuts the degenerate-input gradients that a hard zero would poison. The site-padding masks mim_{i} and MjkeyM^{\text{key}}_{j} are a different object: they mark sites absent from the padded system, not bonds absent from a present system’s graph. Nothing downstream carries a bond mask; bond presence reaches the trunk only through these tokens.

Column attention then attends over the jj index for each (i,𝗁)(i,\mathsf{h}) using per-row learnable queries Q𝗁col∈ℝd𝗁Q^{\text{col}}_{\mathsf{h}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathsf{h}}},

Ki​j,𝗁=WK​RMS​(Bi​j),Vi​j,𝗁=WV​RMS​(Bi​j),αi​j,𝗁col=softmaxj​(Q𝗁col⋅Ki​j,𝗁d𝗁+Mjkey),K_{ij,\mathsf{h}}=W_{K}\,\mathrm{RMS}(B_{ij}),\quad V_{ij,\mathsf{h}}=W_{V}\,\mathrm{RMS}(B_{ij}),\quad\alpha^{\text{col}}_{ij,\mathsf{h}}=\mathrm{softmax}_{j}\!\Bigl(\tfrac{Q^{\text{col}}_{\mathsf{h}}\cdot K_{ij,\mathsf{h}}}{\sqrt{d_{\mathsf{h}}}}+M^{\text{key}}_{j}\Bigr), (S2.16)

where 𝗁∈{1,…,n𝗁}\mathsf{h}\in\{1,\dots,n_{\mathsf{h}}\} is the attention-head index (we use sans-serif to disinguish from the transverse field hh), d𝗁d_{\mathsf{h}} is the per-head width with n𝗁⋅d𝗁=dbondn_{\mathsf{h}}\cdot d_{\mathsf{h}}=d_{\text{bond}}, and WK,WV∈ℝdbond×dbondW_{K},W_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{bond}}\times d_{\text{bond}}} are linear projectors whose outputs split into n𝗁n_{\mathsf{h}} head blocks of width d𝗁d_{\mathsf{h}} indexed by 𝗁\mathsf{h}. Here RMS\mathrm{RMS} is the map of Eq. (S2.12), applied along the bond-feature axis, softmaxj\mathrm{softmax}_{j} normalises over the second site index, and MjkeyM^{\text{key}}_{j} is the key-padding mask which is 00 when site jj is present in the system, and −∞-\infty when it is absent. The kernel computes twice the output head count and gates the heads in bisected pairs,

oi,𝗁=∑jαi​j,𝗁colVi​j,𝗁,ℓiraw=mi⋅[sigmoid(oi(1:n𝗁))⊙oi(n𝗁+1:2​n𝗁)],o_{i,\mathsf{h}}=\sum_{j}\alpha^{\text{col}}_{ij,\mathsf{h}}\,V_{ij,\mathsf{h}},\qquad\ell^{\text{raw}}_{i}=m_{i}\cdot\Bigl[\,\mathrm{sigmoid}\bigl(o_{i}^{(1:n_{\mathsf{h}})}\bigr)\odot o_{i}^{(n_{\mathsf{h}}+1:2n_{\mathsf{h}})}\,\Bigr], (S2.17)

a GLU-style multiplicative gate at the head level [150, 151]. Every attention layer of SM § S2 shares this micro-structure. The descriptor ℓiraw\ell^{\text{raw}}_{i} carries the exchange structure seen from site ii.

The field enters on its own per-site channel. Because each site carries its own hi′′h^{\prime\prime}_{i}, the field is a genuinely local quantity, and we lift its polar input x^ih\hat{x}^{h}_{i} into a Zeeman base through the same two-layer / grouped-norm / two-layer pattern,

zih=GRMS⁡(SiLU⁡(x^ih​W1h)​W2h),ℓiz=mi⋅SiLU⁡(zih​W3h)​W4h,z^{h}_{i}=\mathrm{GRMS}\!\bigl(\mathrm{SiLU}(\hat{x}^{h}_{i}\,W^{h}_{1})\,W^{h}_{2}\bigr),\qquad\ell^{\text{z}}_{i}=m_{i}\cdot\mathrm{SiLU}(z^{h}_{i}\,W^{h}_{3})\,W^{h}_{4}, (S2.18)

with dℓ=128d_{\ell}=128 and, again, every bias zero at initialisation. The field groups learn their own thresholded detectors — field nearly zero, field isotropic, a single dominant axis — in the same way the bond groups do.

The global context pools both views of the system. A first row-attention layer with nqn_{q} learnable global queries Qq,𝗁row∈ℝnq×n𝗁×d𝗁Q^{\text{row}}_{q,\mathsf{h}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{q}\times n_{\mathsf{h}}\times d_{\mathsf{h}}} attends over the bond descriptors ℓraw\ell^{\text{raw}} to give grawg^{\text{raw}}, and a second, structurally identical layer attends over the Zeeman bases ℓz\ell^{\text{z}} to give gzg^{\text{z}}.

Meanwhile the relative weight is already implicit in (J′′,h′′)(J^{\prime\prime},h^{\prime\prime}), and ϕJ​h\phi_{Jh} surfaces it as an explicit bounded feature:

ϕJ​h=[log⁡(1+rJ),log⁡(1+rh)].\phi_{Jh}\;=\;\bigl[\,\log(1{+}r_{J}),\;\log(1{+}r_{h})\bigr]. (S2.19)

The branch is guarded so its gradient signal remains clean on the h=0h=0 majority of the panel. The fusion normalises each pooled view on its own, takes the two derived blocks raw (both are bounded by construction), and closes with an output normalisation,

g=RMS⁡(FFNg​([RMS⁡(graw),RMS⁡(gz),ϕJ​h])).g\;=\;\mathrm{RMS}\Bigl(\mathrm{FFN}_{g}\!\bigl(\bigl[\,\mathrm{RMS}(g^{\text{raw}}),\,\mathrm{RMS}(g^{\text{z}}),\,\phi_{Jh}\,\bigr]\bigr)\Bigr). (S2.20)

On a system that carries no field at all, RMS⁡(gz)\mathrm{RMS}(g^{\text{z}}) is replaced by the fusion’s own absent-field token. The per-site local feature then takes the Zeeman base as its backbone and folds in the bond descriptor and the global context through a pre-norm residual map, each input normalised on its own,

ℓi=mi⋅RMS⁡(ℓiz+FFNℓ​([RMS⁡(ℓiz),RMS⁡(ℓiraw),RMS⁡(g)])),\ell_{i}\;=\;m_{i}\cdot\mathrm{RMS}\Bigl(\,\ell^{\text{z}}_{i}+\mathrm{FFN}_{\ell}\!\bigl(\bigl[\,\mathrm{RMS}(\ell^{\text{z}}_{i}),\,\mathrm{RMS}(\ell^{\text{raw}}_{i}),\,\mathrm{RMS}(g)\,\bigr]\bigr)\Bigr), (S2.21)

and at a zero-field site the first entry is this map’s own absent-field token. The field is the residual base because it is the dominant per-site signal, while the exchange reaches a site only by aggregation over its bonds. Edge cross-conditioning then refines each bond with the new local features, and the global vector enters only as a gentle modulation. The core mixes the bond with its two endpoints, while a FiLM scale and shift read off the global context,

ci​j=FFNe​(RMS⁡[Bi​j,ℓi,ℓj]),[γ,β]=WF​RMS​(g)+bF,γ←0.1​tanh⁡γ,β←0.1​β,c_{ij}=\mathrm{FFN}_{e}\!\bigl(\mathrm{RMS}\bigl[\,B_{ij},\,\ell_{i},\,\ell_{j}\,\bigr]\bigr),\qquad[\gamma,\beta]=W_{F}\,\mathrm{RMS}(g)+b_{F},\quad\gamma\leftarrow 0.1\tanh\gamma,\;\;\beta\leftarrow 0.1\beta, (S2.22)
ei​j=mi​mj⋅RMS⁡(P​Bi​j+(1+γ)​ci​j+β).e_{ij}\;=\;m_{i}m_{j}\cdot\mathrm{RMS}\!\bigl(P\,B_{ij}+(1+\gamma)\,c_{ij}+\beta\bigr). (S2.23)

The FiLM factors start near zero, PP is a bias-free residual projector applied when dbond≠dedged_{\text{bond}}\neq d_{\text{edge}}, and the pair mask is, again, padding alone.

Given the graph structure of the Hamiltonian input, we note here that the featurizer is a GNN in the sense that it performs neighbor aggregation and global pooling. There is, however, no separate message-passing module since attention subsumes the GNN role, framed in a form compatible with our GPU kernel pipeline and natural-gradient optimisers see SM § S4 for details of our engineering.

S2.3 Trunk and per-site leaf builder

Recall that the featurizer of § S2.2 emits three tensors: the per-bond embedding e∈ℝN×N×dee\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times d_{e}}, the per-site local feature ℓ∈ℝN×dℓ\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{\ell}}, and the global context g∈ℝdgg\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{g}}. Both ee and ℓ\ell depend on the Hamiltonian (J,h)(J,h) only through the cached inputs J′′J^{\prime\prime} and h′′h^{\prime\prime} of § S2.1, and every system-context quantity downstream of this point is, by construction, a function of (J′′,h′′)(J^{\prime\prime},h^{\prime\prime}) and therefore a function of (J,h)(J,h). The trunk’s job is to propagate (e,ℓ,g)(e,\ell,g) through LL residual blocks: it maintains all three streams, mixing information across sites and bonds and keeping the global summary current as it does so. We emphasise that this is completely independent functions of spin configuration qq, which enter only once, at a per-site leaf builder that sits between the trunk and the merge tree. As such the per-site antisymmetry constraint of § S1.4,

ψ⁡(…,−qi,…)=−ψ⁡(…,qi,…)for every site ​i,\psi(\dots,-q_{i},\dots)\;=\;-\,\psi(\dots,q_{i},\dots)\qquad\text{for every site }i, (S2.24)

becomes a property of the leaf builder alone, and the expressivity of the trunk is not limited by any symmetry requirement and thus we may use any standard transformer recipe [152].

The trunk is structured by blocks, indexed by β∈{0,1,…,L−1}\beta\in\{0,1,\dots,L-1\}. Let ℓ(β)∈ℝN×dℓ\ell^{(\beta)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{\ell}} and e(β)∈ℝN×N×dee^{(\beta)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times d_{e}} be the per-site and per-bond states at block β\beta, with ℓ(0)=ℓ\ell^{(0)}=\ell and e(0)=ee^{(0)}=e from the featurizer. We write ℓi∈ℝdℓ\ell_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell}} for the row of ℓ(β)\ell^{(\beta)} at site ii and ei​j∈ℝdee_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}} for the bond slot at (i,j)(i,j), dropping the (β)(\beta) superscript when the block is unambiguous.

The global context is the trunk’s third stream, and it is a maintained one. The natural alternative is to broadcast the featurizer’s gg unchanged, as a fixed conditioning signal for every block. But a fixed global summarises the couplings as the featurizer saw them, and that summary grows stale exactly as the trunk’s refinement makes the site and bond states worth summarising. The trunk therefore refreshes gg once per block, from the states the block has just updated. The stream lives on the sphere of unit root-mean-square norm: writing

Norm⁡(x):=xmax⁡(x2¯,ε),x2¯:=1d​∑axa2,\mathrm{Norm}(x)\;:=\;\frac{x}{\sqrt{\max\!\bigl(\overline{x^{2}},\,\varepsilon\bigr)}},\qquad\overline{x^{2}}\;:=\;\tfrac{1}{d}\textstyle\sum_{a}x_{a}^{2}, (S2.25)

for the parameter-free projection ℝd→ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} onto that sphere (the floor ε=10−4\varepsilon=10^{-4} replaces the usual added constant, so the map is exact whenever x2¯≥ε\overline{x^{2}}\geq\varepsilon and sends the origin to itself), the trunk receives the featurizer’s global as g(0)=Norm⁡(g)g^{(0)}=\mathrm{Norm}(g) and returns every update to the same sphere. Norm\mathrm{Norm} carries no parameters; the RMS layers of § S2.2 normalise the same way but carry a learned per-channel scale, and the two should not be conflated.

A block applies three residual sublayers in sequence: an edge-update sublayer on the per-bond stream, then an edge-biased multi-head self-attention (MHA) sublayer and a feed-forward network (FFN) sublayer on the per-site stream; a refresh of the global closes the block. The edge stream moves first,

e(β+1)=e(β)+1L​EdgeUpdate​(RMS⁡(e(β)),ℓ(β)),e^{(\beta+1)}\;=\;e^{(\beta)}\;+\;\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\,\mathrm{EdgeUpdate}\!\bigl(\mathrm{RMS}(e^{(\beta)}),\;\ell^{(\beta)}\bigr), (S2.26)

so that the attention which follows reads fresh bonds: the just-updated e(β+1)e^{(\beta+1)} enters the attention logits as a per-head additive bias, defined below. The per-site stream then takes two residual steps,

ℓ′\displaystyle\ell^{\prime}\; =ℓ(β)+1L​MHA​(RMS⁡(ℓ(β)),e(β+1)),\displaystyle=\;\ell^{(\beta)}\;+\;\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\,\mathrm{MHA}\!\bigl(\mathrm{RMS}(\ell^{(\beta)});\,e^{(\beta+1)}\bigr), (S2.27)
ℓ(β+1)\displaystyle\ell^{(\beta+1)}\; =ℓ′+1L​FFN​(RMS⁡(ℓ′)+Wg​g(β)),\displaystyle=\;\ell^{\prime}\;+\;\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\,\mathrm{FFN}\!\bigl(\mathrm{RMS}(\ell^{\prime})+W_{g}\,g^{(\beta)}\bigr), (S2.28)

and the global closes the block by reading the sites the block has just written,

g(β+1)=Update⁡(g(β),pool⁡(g(β),ℓ(β+1))),g^{(\beta+1)}\;=\;\mathrm{Update}\!\bigl(g^{(\beta)},\;\mathrm{pool}\bigl(g^{(\beta)},\,\ell^{(\beta+1)}\bigr)\bigr), (S2.29)

with pool\mathrm{pool} and Update\mathrm{Update} defined below. In Eq. (S2.27) the semicolon indicates that the map is conditioned on the argument after it; RMS\mathrm{RMS} is the normalisation of § S2.2, applied along the feature axis; and Wg∈ℝdℓ×dgW_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell}\times d_{g}} is a learned projection whose output is broadcast to every site. The global enters the per-site path exactly once, additively, at the FFN’s input. We emphasise that the two per-site steps are sequential residuals (the FFN acts on the attention’s output ℓ′\ell^{\prime}, not on ℓ(β)\ell^{(\beta)}) and that all three sublayers are pre-norm: each reads a normalised copy of its stream and adds its result to the raw stream. The factor 1/L1/\sqrt{L} applies inverse-square-root depth scaling to each residual branch, matching the depth dependence induced by batch normalisation at initialisation [153]. Under the usual independence approximation at initialisation, each additive update contributes variance 𝒪⁡(1/L)\mathcal{O}(1/L) to the running stream, so the cumulative variance across LL blocks stays 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1).

The two maps that refresh the global recur at every later stage of the architecture; the trunk’s instance is the first of many. The pool is a descriptor attention: its query is produced from the current global state and determines the attention weights over the input set. For a set {xi}i=1n\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} of states xi∈ℝdxx_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} and the current global gg,

q𝗁=W𝗁Q​g,k𝗁,i=W𝗁K​RMS​(xi),v𝗁,i=W𝗁V​RMS​(xi),q_{\mathsf{h}}=W^{Q}_{\mathsf{h}}\,g,\qquad k_{\mathsf{h},i}=W^{K}_{\mathsf{h}}\,\mathrm{RMS}(x_{i}),\qquad v_{\mathsf{h},i}=W^{V}_{\mathsf{h}}\,\mathrm{RMS}(x_{i}), (S2.30)
a𝗁,i=softmaxi​(q𝗁⋅k𝗁,idk+Mi),pool⁡(g,{xi})=[∑ia𝗁,i​v𝗁,i]𝗁=1n𝗁∈ℝn𝗁​dv,a_{\mathsf{h},i}=\mathrm{softmax}_{i}\!\Bigl(\tfrac{q_{\mathsf{h}}\cdot k_{\mathsf{h},i}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}+M_{i}\Bigr),\qquad\mathrm{pool}\bigl(g,\{x_{i}\}\bigr)=\Bigl[\,{\textstyle\sum_{i}}a_{\mathsf{h},i}\,v_{\mathsf{h},i}\,\Bigr]_{\mathsf{h}=1}^{n_{\mathsf{h}}}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathsf{h}}d_{v}}, (S2.31)

where 𝗁\mathsf{h} is the sans-serif head index of § S2.2, W𝗁Q∈ℝdk×dgW^{Q}_{\mathsf{h}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d_{g}}, W𝗁K∈ℝdk×dxW^{K}_{\mathsf{h}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d_{x}} and W𝗁V∈ℝdv×dxW^{V}_{\mathsf{h}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{x}} are per-head projectors, [⋅]𝗁[\cdot]_{\mathsf{h}} concatenates the head outputs, and MiM_{i} is the key-padding mask of § S2.2 (00 where the element is present, −∞-\infty where it is absent). This is the featurizer’s row attention with two changes: the learnable queries are replaced by projections of gg, and the head outputs concatenate plainly, without the gate of Eq. (S2.17). We use n𝗁=4n_{\mathsf{h}}=4 heads of width dk=dv=64d_{k}=d_{v}=64, so the pooled reading has width n𝗁​dv=256n_{\mathsf{h}}d_{v}=256, a quarter of the stream’s own width dg=1024d_{g}=1024.

The Hamiltonian’s data streams use the normalised interpolation of nGPT [154]. For a current state xx and candidate Δx\Delta_{x}, let axa_{x} be a learned per-channel gate, write 𝟏\mathbf{1} for the all-ones vector and ⊙\odot for elementwise multiplication, and define logit⁡(r):=log⁡(r/(1−r))\operatorname{logit}(r):=\log(r/(1-r)). Then

α~x:=0.8​sigmoid⁡(ax),ax|init=logit⁡(0.20.8)​𝟏,𝒩x​(x,Δx):=Norm⁡(x+α~x⊙(Norm⁡(Δx)−x)).\widetilde{\alpha}_{x}:=0.8\,\operatorname{sigmoid}(a_{x}),\qquad a_{x}\big|_{\mathrm{init}}=\operatorname{logit}\!\left(\frac{0.2}{0.8}\right)\mathbf{1},\qquad\mathcal{N}_{x}(x,\Delta_{x}):=\mathrm{Norm}\!\Bigl(x+\widetilde{\alpha}_{x}\odot\bigl(\mathrm{Norm}(\Delta_{x})-x\bigr)\Bigr). (S2.32)

Thus every channel starts with interpolation weight 0.20.2 and remains in the open interval (0,0.8)(0,0.8). Throughout the architecture, 𝒩∙\mathcal{N}_{\bullet} denotes this same normalised-interpolation map with an independently learned gate for the named stream. Given a pooled reading pp, the global update reads,

Δg=FFNg​(RMS⁡[Wtap​g,p]),Update⁡(g,p)=𝒩g​(g,Δg).\Delta_{g}=\mathrm{FFN}_{g}\!\bigl(\mathrm{RMS}[W_{\mathrm{tap}}g,p]\bigr),\qquad\mathrm{Update}(g,p)=\mathcal{N}_{g}(g,\Delta_{g}). (S2.33)

The bottleneck WtapW_{\mathrm{tap}} balances the global and pooled entries before the joint RMS normalisation. Figure S3 traces the stream’s stations through the architecture.

The stream is wide, dg=1024d_{g}=1024, and stays wide along the whole ladder; what varies is how the rest of the network reads it. The attention pools and the additive taps (WgW_{g} above, and their analogues downstream) are learned projections by construction. The remaining consumers, the leaf gate, the merge context leg and the root readout hypernet, each read the stream through their own RMS-normalised linear projection to a narrower interface of width 256256; where a later display writes gg as an input to one of these three, it denotes that consumer’s projected copy.

The attention itself is not the vanilla recipe, and both of its deviations recur across the architecture. First, the logits carry the bond stream:

logit𝗁,i​j=q𝗁,i⋅k𝗁,jd𝗁+MLP⁡(RMS⁡(ei​jβ+1))\mathrm{logit}_{\mathsf{h},\,ij}\;=\;\frac{q_{\mathsf{h},i}\cdot k_{\mathsf{h},j}}{\sqrt{d_{\mathsf{h}}}}+\;\mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{RMS}(e^{\beta+1}_{ij})) (S2.34)

with β𝗁:ℝde→ℝ\beta_{\mathsf{h}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}\to\mathbb{R} a small per-head scalar projector, so a head can attend along the interaction graph rather than by content alone. Second, the heads are gated in bisected pairs, the GLU micro-structure the featurizer’s attention layers already carry (Eq. (S2.17)). The level attention of § S2.4.4 and the contextualizer’s slot attention [155] reuse it in turn. Figure S4 draws one block.

The edge-update map itself combines a direct-pair contribution with a three-part aggregate that pools over every site kk acting as a third vertex. Concretely, its increment at bond (i,j)(i,j) is

EdgeUpdate​(RMS⁡(e),ℓ)i​j=FFN⁡([pairi​j,Pi​j]),\mathrm{EdgeUpdate}\bigl(\mathrm{RMS}(e),\,\ell\bigr)_{ij}\;=\;\mathrm{FFN}\!\bigl(\bigl[\mathrm{pair}_{ij},\,P_{ij}\bigr]\bigr), (S2.35)

where pairi​j:=[ei​j,ℓi,ℓj]\mathrm{pair}_{ij}:=[\,e_{ij},\ell_{i},\ell_{j}\,] is the direct-pair feature, i.e. the bond together with its two endpoints, and Pi​j∈ℝdcP_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{c}} is the three-part aggregate,

Pi​j,c=1N​∑k=1NΨcL​(pairi​k)​ΨcR​(pairk​j),c∈{1,…,dc}.P_{ij,\,c}\;=\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\Psi^{\mathrm{L}}_{c}(\mathrm{pair}_{ik})\,\Psi^{\mathrm{R}}_{c}(\mathrm{pair}_{kj}),\qquad c\in\{1,\dots,d_{c}\}. (S2.36)

The two embedders ΨL,ΨR:ℝde+2​dℓ→ℝdc\Psi^{\mathrm{L}},\Psi^{\mathrm{R}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}+2d_{\ell}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{c}} are independent SiLU MLPs that act on the left leg i→ki\to k and the right leg k→jk\to j of the triangle (i,k,j)(i,k,j). The 1/N1/\sqrt{N} prefactor keeps the variance of Pi​jP_{ij} at 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) as NN grows. Sites kk that do not complete a physical triangle with (i,j)(i,j) enter through legs carrying the absent-bond tokens of Eq. (S2.15), which the embedders learn to discount; absence is a representable input here, not a hard zero. The update costs 𝒪⁡(N2​de​dc)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}d_{e}d_{c}) flops per layer, which is the same asymptotic order as the pair-feature attention already in the block.

This is the triangular update pattern of AlphaFold’s Evoformer [156], adapted from residue-pair representations to coupling graphs. We opt for this three-part update because it is well suited to handle frustrated systems. On a triangular antiferromagnet, a kagome lattice, or any J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} chain whose nearest- and next-nearest-neighbour bonds close into triangles, two bonds can share endpoint features and still sit in physically distinct environments. Thus the bond’s effective behaviour is set by the triangle of competing couplings it belongs to, not by its endpoints alone. Without Pi​jP_{ij}, Eq. (S2.35) reduces to the pair-only form standard in message-passing GNNs, which collapses such bonds into a single representation. With Pi​jP_{ij}, the FFN sees the full multiset {(pairi​k,pairk​j):k}\{(\mathrm{pair}_{ik},\mathrm{pair}_{kj}):k\} of triangle completions and separates them.

In graph-theoretic language, the pair-only limit of Eq. (S2.35) is 1-Weisfeiler–Lehman in distinguishing power on the line graph, which is the level at which most off-the-shelf message-passing GNNs operate. The triangular aggregate Pi​jP_{ij} lifts the update strictly to the 2-WL refinement on pairs [157, 158] which distinguishes any two bonds whose triangle structures differ.

After the LL blocks the global context stream takes one further update, this time reading the bonds rather than the sites. Placing all N2N^{2} bond states under a single softmax would be wasteful, so the reading is factored through row and column descriptors,

ri=pool(g,ei⋅(L)),cj=pool(g,e⋅j(L)),p=pool(g,{r1,…,rN,c1,…,cN}),r_{i}=\mathrm{pool}\bigl(g,\,e^{(L)}_{i\,\cdot}\bigr),\qquad c_{j}=\mathrm{pool}\bigl(g,\,e^{(L)}_{\cdot\,j}\bigr),\qquad p=\mathrm{pool}\bigl(g,\,\{r_{1},\dots,r_{N},\,c_{1},\dots,c_{N}\}\bigr), (S2.37)

followed by the update g↦Update⁡(g,p)g\mapsto\mathrm{Update}(g,p) of Eq. (S2.33). The row and column descriptors compress the N2N^{2} bonds to 2​N2N summaries, and the second-stage pool reads those; every pool here runs under the physical-site mask. The same factored reading recurs whenever the global reads an edge field downstream.

The trunk thus emits the triple (e(L),ℓ(L),g)(e^{(L)},\ell^{(L)},g), where gg now denotes the stream’s post-trunk value. Each of these is, by construction, a deterministic function of the featurizer’s outputs (e(0),ℓ(0),g(0))(e^{(0)},\ell^{(0)},g^{(0)}), which are themselves deterministic functions of the cached inputs J′′J^{\prime\prime} and h′′h^{\prime\prime} of the raw Hamiltonian (J,h)(J,h).

Hence the whole pipeline up to here is a deterministic function of (J,h)(J,h) alone, and the spin configuration qq coordinates have not yet entered the model. The per-site ℓ(L)\ell^{(L)} feeds the leaf builder defined immediately below, refined on the way by a leaf contextualizer that the tree readout introduces (§ S2.4); the per-bond e(L)e^{(L)} re-enters at the level-edge attention variant of the merge tree (§ S2.4); and the global stream continues through every later stage, refreshed at each in the same pool-and-update pattern.

S2.3.1 The per-site leaf builder

The leaf builder is the unique entry point for the spin configuration qq: everything upstream of it is a function of the Hamiltonian alone, and everything downstream of it is a function of qq as well. It acts one site at a time. Given the contextualized per-slot state ℓ^i∈ℝdℓ\hat{\ell}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell}} — the trunk’s per-site outputs, refined over the readout’s slot frame by the leaf contextualizer whose construction we give in § S2.4.3, the global context g∈ℝ256g\in\mathbb{R}^{256}, the stream’s refreshed post-context value read through the leaf’s own projection (§ S2.3), and the quaternion-embedded spin qi∈SU⁡(2)↪ℝ4q_{i}\in\mathrm{SU}(2)\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{4} with ∑a(qia)2=1\sum_{a}(q_{i}^{a})^{2}=1 (§ S1.1), it produces a per-site carrier

ui(0)∈ℝduu_{i}^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{u}}

that encodes everything site ii contributes to the wavefunction amplitude. The NN carriers {ui(0)}i=1N\{u_{i}^{(0)}\}_{i=1}^{N} are the leaves of the tree readout of § S2.4, which contracts them into the single scalar log⁡ψθ​(q)∈ℂ\log\psi_{\theta}(q)\in\mathbb{C}; the width dud_{u} is set by that readout.

Recall from the opening of § S2.3 that, because qq enters nowhere else, the per-site antisymmetry constraint (S2.24) becomes a property of this one map. The design problem is therefore: build ui(0)u_{i}^{(0)} as a function of (ℓ^i,g,qi)(\hat{\ell}_{i},g,q_{i}) that is expressive in all three arguments yet exactly odd under qi→−qiq_{i}\to-q_{i}. Our solution keeps the two parities on separate legs and couples them one way only, which keeps the necessary properties of the sector argument we made in § S1.4, namely that the model is odd and linear in each quaternion qiq_{i}. Indeed, the qq-leg is linear in qiq_{i} because it is bias-free (since a constant would be even), and the other leg is an unconstrained function of (ℓ^i,g)(\hat{\ell}_{i},g). The two legs meet in a product, never in a sum, thus preserving the central oddness of the model. Figure S5 draws one site’s unit.

Let BiasFreeLinear⁡(din,dout)\mathrm{BiasFreeLinear}(d_{\mathrm{in}},d_{\mathrm{out}}) denote a linear map with no additive bias. The qq-leg is a single bias-free lift of the quaternion into what we call the odd stream,

zi:=Wq→z​qi∈ℝdo,Wq→z∈BiasFreeLinear⁡(4,do),z_{i}\;:=\;W_{q\to z}\,q_{i}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{d_{o}},\qquad W_{q\to z}\in\mathrm{BiasFreeLinear}(4,\,d_{o}), (S2.38)

with dod_{o} the odd-stream width. The absence of a bias is not a stylistic choice: an additive constant is even under qi→−qiq_{i}\to-q_{i}, and (S2.38) is the first link in a chain whose oddness must be exact — this is the bias-free constraint of § S1.4 in its simplest form.

The even leg maps the per-slot and global context to a gate vector,

mi:=Wh​[ℓ^i,g]∈ℝR,m_{i}\;:=\;W_{h}\,\bigl[\,\hat{\ell}_{i},\,g\,\bigr]\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{R}, (S2.39)

where here [⋅,⋅][\cdot\,,\cdot] denotes concatenation, Wh∈ℝR×(dℓ+256)W_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times(d_{\ell}+256)}, and RR is a rank hyperparameter we return to in a moment. Since ℓ^i\hat{\ell}_{i} and gg are functions of the Hamiltonian alone (§ S2.3), carrying no qq-dependence whatsoever, the gate mim_{i} is qq-independent by construction — in particular invariant under qi→−qiq_{i}\to-q_{i}.

The two legs meet in a Hadamard (elementwise) product inside an RR-dimensional bottleneck, followed by a bias-free output projection,

ui(0)=U⁡(mi⊙V​zi)∈ℝdu,V∈ℝR×do,U∈ℝdu×R,\;u_{i}^{(0)}\;=\;U\bigl(\,m_{i}\odot Vz_{i}\,\bigr)\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{d_{u}},\;\qquad V\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d_{o}},\quad U\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{u}\times R}, (S2.40)

with VV and UU bias-free for the same parity reason as Wq→zW_{q\to z}. Collecting the linear maps shows what (S2.40) really is:

ui(0)=M⁡(ℓ^i,g)​zi,M⁡(ℓ^i,g):=U​diag​(mi)​V∈ℝdu×do.u_{i}^{(0)}\;=\;M(\hat{\ell}_{i},\,g)\;\,z_{i},\qquad M(\hat{\ell}_{i},\,g)\;:=\;U\,\mathrm{diag}(m_{i})\,V\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{d_{u}\times d_{o}}. (S2.41)

The even leg emits the weights of a linear map of rank at most RR, and the spin is read out through that map. In ML terms this is a small hypernetwork [159], one network outputs the parameters of the map applied by another, with the Hadamard gate playing the role of FiLM-style multiplicative conditioning [160] in a rank-RR bottleneck. In physics terms, the even sector dresses the odd sector without ever mixing into it. The same three-matrix shape U(⋅⊙V⋅)U(\,\cdot\,\odot V\cdot\,) reappears as the residual hypernet at every merge node of the tree (§ S2.4.3); the leaf builder is its first and simplest instance.

Finally, we normalise the carrier to unit root-mean-square while banking the divided-out magnitude in the log-scale stream. To that end, we may write

Bi:=M⁡(ℓ^i,g)​Wq→z,ui,raw(0):=Bi​qi,B_{i}\;:=\;M(\hat{\ell}_{i},g)\,W_{q\to z},\qquad u_{i,\mathrm{raw}}^{(0)}\;:=\;B_{i}q_{i}, (S2.42)

to define

ri(0):=(ui,raw(0))2¯+ε,ui(0):=ui,raw(0)ri(0),si(0):=log⁡ri(0),r_{i}^{(0)}\;:=\;\sqrt{\overline{\bigl(u_{i,\mathrm{raw}}^{(0)}\bigr)^{2}}+\varepsilon},\qquad u_{i}^{(0)}\;:=\;\frac{u_{i,\mathrm{raw}}^{(0)}}{r_{i}^{(0)}},\qquad s_{i}^{(0)}\;:=\;\log r_{i}^{(0)}, (S2.43)

where,

(ri(0))2=1du​qi⊤​Bi⊤​Bi​qi+ε,x2¯:=1du​∑axa2.\bigl(r_{i}^{(0)}\bigr)^{2}\;=\;\frac{1}{d_{u}}\,q_{i}^{\top}B_{i}^{\top}B_{i}q_{i}+\varepsilon,\qquad\overline{x^{2}}:=\frac{1}{d_{u}}\sum_{a}x_{a}^{2}. (S2.44)
